html:
The Pecora Commission was a US Senate inquiry into Wall Street, held from 1932 to 1934, that exposed the practices behind the 1929 crash. It is named for its chief counsel, Ferdinand Pecora, a former New York prosecutor.

At the start the Senate banking committee found little. Pecora took over in early 1933 and called the top bankers to testify in public. The hearings showed that National City Bank's Charles Mitchell had sold shaky bonds to small investors, and that he had paid no income tax for 1929 by selling stock to his wife at a loss. J. P. Morgan Jr. and his partners paid no tax for two years. Albert Wiggin of Chase had bet against his own bank's shares.

The press covered it daily, and public trust in bankers fell. It gave Roosevelt's New Deal the support to pass Glass-Steagall, the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which set up the SEC.

The case of Mitchell's 1929 margin loan was a central example. The inquiry is a model for later congressional investigations of finance.
